concepts.title: Protein Data Types and Their Uses
concepts.definition: Protein informatics feeds on every raw form a protein can take - micrographs of heat-denatured aggregates, solutions for physico-chemical study, MALDI sequence fragments, assembled sequences, PDB crystal files, interaction maps, NMR and mass spectra, and hypothetical proteins read straight out of genomes - each type answering a different question from marker design to drug-target mapping.
concepts.key_idea: Match the raw data type to the question: crystals reveal interactions, fragments rebuild full sequences, and genome reads reveal proteins never seen in a lab.
question_patterns: list any four types of raw protein data and one use of each
what is a hypothetical protein and from where can its existence be inferred
how do fragmented MALDI sequences help in finding a full length protein sequence
which databases supply raw protein data for informatics analysis
name the machine learning techniques used in protein informatics analysis
how does network mapping of proteins assist treatment design

solution_steps.explain: Image, solution, sequence, structure file, interaction record or spectrum.
Wavelet image analysis, homology calculation, structure optimisation, machine learning or network mapping follows.
The analysis returns markers, kinetics, structures, functions or therapeutic targets.

worked_examples.q: Which file format stores solved protein 3D coordinates: PDB or FASTQ?

concepts.title: Primary Structure Descriptors of a Protein
concepts.definition: From sequence alone the ProtParam tool of ExPASy prices a protein's habits: its isoelectric point calls the molecule acidic below seven or basic above, the aliphatic index tallies aliphatic side-chain volume as a thermal-stability credit, an instability index under forty predicts a stable protein in the test tube, and the GRAVY value - hydropathy scores summed over the residue count - forecasts how sociably the chain meets water.
concepts.key_idea: Divide the summed hydropathy by residue count for GRAVY, take the aliphatic share as a percent, and read seven and forty as the pH and stability pivots.
question_patterns: a peptide of 120 residues has hydropathy values summing to 96 - compute its GRAVY value
what does an instability index above 40 predict about a protein in a test tube
a protein shows pI of 5.2 - is it acidic or basic and which purification method suits the pI
how is the aliphatic index defined and why does it favour thermal stability
which server computes isoelectric point extinction coefficient and GRAVY value together
what does a low GRAVY value suggest about a protein's interaction with water

solution_steps.explain: GRAVY divides the summed amino-acid hydropathy by the residue count.
Aliphatic residues as a percent of the chain give the aliphatic index input.

worked_examples.q: An instability index under what value predicts a stable protein: forty or four?

concepts.title: Predicting Secondary and 3D Protein Structures
concepts.definition: When no crystal exists, computation fills in: APSSP, CFSSP, SOPMA and GOR forecast helices and sheets; homology modelling on MODELLER or SWISS-MODEL copies a solved relative; threading forces the chain onto a known backbone for fold prediction; QUARK builds the model de novo from sequence alone, and InterPRO or CDD carves the chain into domains recorded later as PDB coordinates.
concepts.key_idea: Close relatives give global folds by homology, distant hints give local folds by threading, and sequence alone still yields a de novo model.
question_patterns: name two tools each for homology modelling fold prediction and de novo structure prediction
which tools predict protein secondary structure and why is that step useful
how does threading differ from homology modelling in what it requires
what is a domain and which tools scan for recurring domains
trace the flowchart from protein sequence to a 3D model when a homologue exists in PDB and when none does
what does a PDB file record about a computationally modelled structure

solution_steps.explain: A homologous solved structure enables homology modelling; none pushes toward threading or de novo.
High homology gives global folds, low homology local folds, threading tests physical viability, QUARK assembles from scratch.
Domain scans and PDB-format coordinates complete the annotated 3D model.

worked_examples.q: Copying a solved relative's fold is which modelling: homology or de novo?

concepts.title: Cheminformatics and Virtual Screening
concepts.definition: Cheminformatics aims computational power at chemistry - storing property tables, reaction routes and 3D structures - so that virtual screening can score and rank millions of real and hypothetical molecules against ADME and docking filters before any synthesis; the CAS registry alone holds over 219 million substances alongside 70 million sequences and billions of property values.
concepts.key_idea: Screen first in silico and synthesize only the survivors; the CAS numbers show the scale such filters must face.
question_patterns: how many organic and inorganic substances does the CAS registry host and how many sequences accompany them
define virtual screening and list the filter classes it may include
what is computer-aided drug design and which industries use cheminformatics daily
what are virtual libraries of molecules and why can they contain compounds that do not exist
name any four popular chemical databases and what each specialises in
which database would you consult for binding affinity of small molecules to protein targets

solution_steps.explain: Real and virtual compounds pool into searchable chemical databases.
General ADME filters, ligand-based pharmacophore searches and structure-based docking narrow the field.
Only top-ranked candidates proceed to synthesis and biological testing.

worked_examples.q: Scoring millions of molecules computationally before synthesis is called what screening: virtual or physical?

concepts.title: Molecular Graphs and Substructure Searching
concepts.definition: Chemicals live in computers as molecular graphs - atoms as nodes, bonds as edges - the same node-edge logic that later draws pathways like glycolysis; searching them often runs in two stages, a bitstring screen that discards obvious non-matches, then a subgraph isomorphism test that confirms every atom and bond of the query sits inside the candidate, and reaction searches add atom mapping from reactants to products.
concepts.key_idea: Filter fast with bitstrings, confirm exactly with subgraph isomorphism, and map every atom to its product in reaction searches.
question_patterns: how are chemical structures stored in computers - explain the node and edge analogy
what is subgraph isomorphism and why does a two-stage search save effort
what are bitstrings and how do they help screen molecule libraries
what does atom mapping achieve in a reaction database search
how could you query all reactions that use glucose near 37 degrees celsius
why is storing a molecule as a jpg or pdf of little use for deep browsing of bond angles

solution_steps.explain: Represent atoms as nodes and bonds as edges.
Binary bitstrings encode features and eliminate most candidates.
Subgraph isomorphism embeds the query into survivors; atom mapping completes reaction queries.

worked_examples.q: Chemicals live in computers as molecular what, with atoms as nodes and bonds as edges?

concepts.title: Pharmacophore Models of Ligand Recognition
concepts.definition: A pharmacophore is not a molecule but the abstract set of steric and electronic features - charged groups, rings, hydrophobic patches - arranged in space that a ligand needs to wake a biological target; modelling these features explains how structurally unlike ligands can still dock the same receptor.
concepts.key_idea: Collect the features, not the atoms - a pharmacophore maps what must be present and where, not what the molecule is.
question_patterns: define pharmacophore as per IUPAC and explain why it is not a physical molecule
which spatial features build a 3D pharmacophore model
how does a pharmacophore explain diverse ligands docking one receptor
distinguish pharmacophore points from pharmacophore models
what role do steric and electronic features play in molecular recognition of a ligand
how does pharmacophore based search fit into virtual screening

solution_steps.explain: Note charge, ring and hydrophobic features with their spatial orientation.
Keep the arrangement, drop the specific scaffold - that is the pharmacophore.
Search libraries for any molecule satisfying the feature pattern.

worked_examples.q: A pharmacophore collects the steric and electronic what a ligand needs: features or atoms?

concepts.title: Lipinski's Rule of Five Screening
concepts.definition: Christopher Lipinski's 1997 yardstick flags oral-drug potential: at most five hydrogen-bond donors, at most ten acceptors, molecular weight below five hundred daltons and log P below five, with no more than one violation tolerated and scores under three dropping out of further analysis; intramuscular and intravenous drugs and natural products escape the rule.
concepts.key_idea: Subtract each limit from the measured value - a positive excess marks a violation against donors, acceptors, weight or log P.
question_patterns: state the four criteria of Lipinski's rule of five for an orally active drug
a compound weighs 640 daltons - by how much does it exceed the Lipinski weight limit
a molecule has 7 hydrogen bond donors - how many donors over the limit is that
how many violations of the rule of five can a compound still carry and pass
which compounds are exempt from the rule of five and which routes of administration
what RO5 score range disqualifies a compound from further analysis

solution_steps.explain: Subtract 500 daltons from the molecular weight; a positive value is a violation.
Subtract the donor limit of five from the donor count.

worked_examples.q: Lipinski's rule caps molecular weight below how many daltons: 500 or 5000?

concepts.title: The Drug Development Pipeline Timeline
concepts.definition: A new medicine walks a long road: discovery alone consumes seven to eight years screening thousands of compounds, development trims the field to one to five candidates over one to five years, and clinical trials test the single survivor through phases I to III across five to six years before regulatory approval and patient care.
concepts.key_idea: Add the three stage durations to price the whole lab-to-market journey.
question_patterns: a pipeline spends 7 years in discovery 3 in development and 6 in trials - compute the total journey time
how many compounds enter discovery and how many survive into clinical trials on average
define lead compound hit and false positive in the vocabulary of screening
what is high throughput screening and how many compounds can it test
which stages separate a new chemical entity from regulatory approval
what is off target activity and why does it matter in drug safety

solution_steps.explain: Discovery and development durations combine first.
Clinical phases complete the timeline.

worked_examples.q: Discovery alone consumes how many years: seven to eight or just one?

worked_examples.question_pattern: A protein of {residues} residues has hydropathy values summing to {hydropathy_sum} and contains {aliphatic_residues} aliphatic residues. Compute its GRAVY value and the aliphatic percent of the chain.

extracted_variables.aliphatic_residues: count of aliphatic residues A V I L

solution_template.explain: GRAVY is the hydropathy sum divided by residues.
Aliphatic residues as a percent of the whole chain.

worked_examples.question_pattern: A drug candidate passes through {discovery_years} years of discovery, {development_years} years of development and {clinical_years} years of clinical trials. Find the total years from idea to regulatory approval.

solution_template.explain: Discovery plus development give the pre-clinical span.
